rows: I have received your last transmission
I have received, understand, and will comply
My transmission is ended; response expected
This exchange is complete; no reply expected
NOT "repeat" — "repeat" has specific military meaning (repeat artillery fire)
Separating ATC instruction from other content
"Speedbird 123, cleared to land runway 27L, BREAK, surface wind 270 at 8"
An error was made; the correct version follows
Request each phrase repeated twice (poor channel)
Inform me that you have received and understood
The person in command (not the radio operator) — "Sunray Actual" = commander himself
Numerals follow (signal to interpret following as numbers)
What is my signal quality? (response: ROGER/WEAK/UNREADABLE etc.)
Go ahead, I am ready to copy
I must pause; I will return
No further traffic to send (end of message indicator)
Distress signal (life in danger); repeat three times
Urgency signal (urgent, not immediate danger); repeat three times
Safety signal (navigation hazard warning); repeat three times
Silence requested — distress working in progress
Use the ICAO/NATO word, speak slowly, and separate ambiguous letters.
The point is intelligibility across accents and noise, not mnemonic charm.
Use standardized pronunciations such as `niner`, digit grouping, and readback when needed.
Number errors are often more dangerous than letter errors.
`Roger` does not mean yes or will comply.
Use `Wilco` when you understand and will comply.
`Roger Wilco` is redundant in disciplined procedure.
Use `Say again` with the missing part if known.
Avoid `repeat` in contexts where it can mean fire again.
Use `Over` when expecting a reply and `Out` when ending communications.
Ask "Radio check, how do you read, over?" and expect a readability/strength response.
"Loud and clear" is qualitative; formal nets may require numeric reports.
Use `Mayday` three times, identity, position, distress nature, persons, and assistance needed.
Distress format prioritizes location and actionable risk over completeness.
